title: Alpha School's Theranos Problem
author: Van Schoales
summary: Schoales walks past an Alpha School storefront in Austin, is irritated by its marketing, and then does the thing the marketing does not invite: he checks the claims. He establishes his own standing as someone sympathetic to school redesign, having piloted Apple Classroom of Tomorrow in the late 1980s and founded an Expeditionary Learning charter school, which makes his verdict harder to dismiss as reflexive skepticism. The analogy he settles on is Theranos: a sleek product promising to replace a laborious process, sold on figures no independent party has checked. He raises two specific objections. The first is arithmetic, borrowed from Jared Cooney Horvath, that acceleration at Alpha's advertised rate would have students finishing K-12 in early elementary school. The second is that the MAP and SAT numbers mean little absent a matched comparison group, which matters enormously when tuition reaches 75,000 dollars and every family in the building went looking for the school. His policy concern is not the private market but the voucher and tax-credit programs that would route public money to unaudited claims.
points: Grounds the critique in the author's own history with education innovation, including piloting Apple Classroom of Tomorrow and founding an Expeditionary Learning charter school.

Argues the MAP and SAT claims are close to meaningless without a matched comparison group, given tuition as high as 75,000 dollars and a fully self-selected parent population.
Shifts the stakes from private choice to public accountability, warning that voucher and tax-credit programs with no results requirement could funnel millions into the expansion.
quotes: I’ve been around the education innovation block a few times, having started my teaching career in Silicon Valley in the late 1980s.

As I read more about Alpha School’s design and its founder, MacKenzie Price, I was struck by how bizarrely similar it seemed to Theranos, Elizabeth Holmes’s Silicon Valley start-up, which claimed that with just a small finger prick, its sleek, Apple-like machine could describe everything needed to understand a person’s health.
Alpha School claims it needs only two hours of instructional time a day and no teacher, and that it does a better job of preparing students than any other public or private school.

As the education neuroscientist Jared Cooney Horvath has pointed out, if learning could really be accelerated at the rates Alpha claims, students would finish all of K–12 by the second year of elementary school.
No outside study supports any of it, and the MAP and SAT numbers are close to meaningless without knowing whether Alpha students are being compared with students of similar background.

You would think the amazing Alpha results would lead to teams of researchers from Stanford and other research organizations comparing Alpha students with matched peers, trying to understand the school’s secret sauce. Instead, we have boatloads of Theranos-style marketing.
Unfortunately, with the growth of state voucher and tax-credit programs that carry no accountability for results, Alpha is positioned to draw millions of tax dollars into its expansion.
I am happy to keep an open mind if Alpha opens its books and classrooms to outside researchers and independent evaluation.
